titre: The Myth That Makes Bismarck the Inventor of Retirement at Sixty-Five
accroche: They say Bismarck set retirement at sixty-five, his own age. Germany in 1889 set it at seventy, and he was seventy-four.
contenu_vulgarise:
Berlin, 1889. The Reichstag passes the law on old-age and disability insurance, the last floor of an edifice built in three laws since 1883: health insurance first, accident insurance next, retirement last. It is the world's first public, compulsory old-age insurance system. It is often repeated that it set the retirement age at sixty-five because that was the age of the chancellor who wanted it, Otto von Bismarck. The story is false on almost every point.

## A Number That Isn't Sixty-Five

The 1889 text sets the age at which benefits open at seventy, not sixty-five. At the time, Bismarck is seventy-four: he has thus already passed by four years the age he is supposed to have chosen for himself. The age only drops to sixty-five in 1916, twenty-seven years later, under Wilhelm II, eighteen years after Bismarck's death in 1898. And average life expectancy in Germany in the 1880s is around forty: the old-age pension therefore benefits, at first, only a minority of workers.

## What Bismarck Himself Admitted Wanting

The real motive, by contrast, is no myth. Bismarck has just had the Social Democratic Party banned by the 1878 law, without managing to reduce its electoral influence. In an imperial message read to the Reichstag on November 17, 1881, he proposes another path: no longer merely to repress, but also to persuade. He will even admit it openly, in a phrase that the Otto von Bismarck Foundation has preserved and translated: “My idea was to convince the working classes, or should I say, to bribe them, to regard the state as a social institution.”

The three laws follow one another. Health insurance, at the end of May 1883, financed two-thirds by employees and one-third by employers. Accident insurance, in July 1884, entirely at the employers' expense. Old-age and disability insurance, in June 1889, financed in equal parts by employers and employees, supplemented by a state subsidy. Between 1885 and 1913, the number of insured Germans rises from four million three hundred thousand to thirteen million six hundred thousand.

Germany, by going first, supplied a model that most Western pension systems later adapted in their turn, without always retaining either the exact date, the original motive, or the real figure.

carte.punch: Bismarck didn't choose sixty-five for retirement: he was already four years past it
carte.idee: The 1889 German scheme, the world's first public pension system, set the retirement age at seventy, not sixty-five. Bismarck, who was seventy-four, was aiming less at generosity than at workers' loyalty to the state, against the Social Democratic Party.

quiz.question: Why is the age of sixty-five, often attributed to Bismarck, misleading as a description of his 1889 pension scheme?
choix: Because the 1889 scheme actually set the retirement age at seventy, not sixty-five
Because Bismarck never personally supported creating old-age insurance in Germany
Because the 1889 German old-age insurance applied only to civil servants of the Prussian state
Because no text had set a retirement age before the German reform of 1916
quiz.explication: The 1889 text opened benefits at seventy, and Bismarck was seventy-four at the time of the vote. The age only dropped to sixty-five in 1916, under Wilhelm II, eighteen years after Bismarck's death in 1898.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What political development leads Bismarck to propose social legislation in 1881 rather than repression alone?
choix: The loss of the conservative majority in the Reichstag in the 1881 elections
A general strike of Ruhr workers, put down by the army in 1880
The failure of the 1878 law against the Social Democratic Party to reduce its electoral influence
Pressure from British unions, which had just won a similar law
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bismarck had the Social Democratic Party banned in 1878 without managing to reduce its electoral influence: the 1881 imperial message then proposes to persuade rather than merely repress.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How is the financing of the workplace accident insurance, introduced in July 1884, divided?
choix: Two-thirds paid by employees and one-third by employers
Entirely paid by employers, with no contribution from employees
Paid in equal parts by employers and employees, with a state subsidy
Paid solely by a tax levied on large industrial companies
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Workplace accident insurance, introduced in July 1884, was entirely at the employers' expense, unlike the 1883 health insurance or the 1889 pension.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many Germans were insured by this social system in 1913, compared with 1885?
choix: About two million in 1885, a little over five million in 1913
About one million in 1885, about eight million in 1913
About six million in 1885, about ten million in 1913
About four million three hundred thousand in 1885, thirteen million six hundred thousand in 1913
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The number of insured Germans rises from four million three hundred thousand in 1885 to thirteen million six hundred thousand in 1913, a sign of the system's rapid expansion.
